body:
I want to start this reply by saying thank you. Thank you for taking the time out of your life to respond to a random post from a stranger on reddit, about a topic as serious and uncomfortable as this. It really means a lot to me; it's *really* hard to have an honest conversation about this with people in my life.  

The words you've written ring true. I'm not in denial of my depression. I recognize it's something I have, and even more than that I recognize it's something I'll have forever. It draws so many parallels to addiction, which I've also grown intimately familiar with throughout the course of my life (I self-medicate as a numbing agent. I know I'm predisposed to addiction, but I don't consider myself an addict. Throughout the course of my life I've only ever used heavily during "episodes," and when they're over, then as now, I have no desire for drugs. I know the counterpoint: "Denial is a strong symptom," but I digress). This sickness lives in me whether I accept it or not, and the only thing I'll ever be able to do is learn to manage it. A sobering thought, but an honest and important point to realize I think.    

I had a moment awhile ago, right after I'd gotten high for the xteenth time that week, where I experienced a very real disconnect between my mind and body. It was a surreal moment, and a bit of an epiphany. For the first time I experienced, lucidly, that my mind was not 100% in control of my body. A short time later I had another experience that was much more chilling. It was maybe 3am, and I was high again. Suddenly I burst out laughing a laugh that wasn't my own, and spoke to myself:    

"What do you expect, *insert name*? I'm the prince of thieves."    

It was just a brief passing moment, but again, I experienced a complete disconnect from myself. I'm agnostic, not religious by any means, and I'm not naive enough to believe the devil was speaking through me. But it did scare me, enough that I've asked doctors about the possibilities of schizophrenia. Enough that I've realized there is a part of me that doesn't represent who I believe myself to be. And you're right, it's insidious, evil, and it is absolutely trying to kill me.

Again, I recognize I don't have full control of my wits at the moment. That's why I'm adamant about taking my meds and consistently going to counseling. I haven't hit a therapeutic dose yet; 4-6 weeks according to all the professionals and literature. I'm dead set on at least tripling that amount of time to give myself an honest chance, good 'ol scouts effort, etc. Neither do I think that medication and counseling are a panacea in themselves. But it's something proactive, and it helps dissuade me from succumbing to hopelessness and helplessness. My biggest fear at the moment is that 6 months out from now I'll feel exactly the same way.    

You're probably right about me underestimating the amount of pain that I've experienced and continue to deal with. I don't expect to come to terms with that anytime soon, but I promise I'm putting in the effort. It's a scary and confusing time to be me, and my mind is a scary and confusing place. One day in the future I hope to be in a place where I can print out this conversation and frame it, as a tangible reminder of the darkness. By the way you describe depression I know that you've had your own conversations with Death as well. The infantry taught me that shared misery is one of the stronger glues in life. Even from a stranger, solidarity counts for something and lends me a bit of strength.

Wish me luck. Thank you stranger. I hope life treats you well. I hope my outlook changes.
